items.title: History Cannot Decide
items.question: A firm keeps funding a failing product because of what it has already invested. What is the irrelevant factor?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Money already gone cannot be recovered, so only future costs and benefits should guide the choice.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the sunk cost. Letting past spending decide is throwing good resources after bad.
items.lessonContent:
Past costs cannot be recovered.
Decide from what lies ahead.
Loss makes quitting feel like waste.
Reframe: the waste already happened.
Share this: name one commitment you would refuse if starting fresh today.

items.title: Climbing Further
items.question: The more a team invests in a failing course, the harder it becomes to stop. What tendency is this?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Growing investment creates pressure to justify it by pressing on.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is escalation of commitment. Each added stake raises the psychological cost of admitting the error.
items.lessonContent:
Investment can trap rather than liberate.
Each added stake raises the exit cost.
Pride resists admitting a mistake.
Set exit conditions in advance.
Share this: decide one stopping condition before you invest further.

items.title: Not the Same Plane
items.question: A supersonic aircraft proved unprofitable but governments kept funding it. Which fallacy does this nickname?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The project was continued largely because so much had already been spent.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the Concorde fallacy. It names the error of letting unrecoverable spending drive present decisions.
items.lessonContent:
Named cases encode a lesson.
Past cost is not a reason to continue.
History offers cautionary examples.
Learn from costly precedent.
Share this: find one project that continued mainly because it had already started.

items.title: Loss Feels Worse
items.question: Why do losses discourage people more than equivalent gains encourage them?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Losing feels roughly twice as bad as gaining the same amount feels good.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is loss aversion. It helps explain why people cling to failing ventures to avoid realising a loss.
items.lessonContent:
Losses weigh more than equal gains.
This asymmetry shapes decisions.
Anticipate the sting before committing.
Ask whether the fear is proportionate.
Share this: notice one choice today driven by avoiding a loss.

items.title: Throwing Good After Bad
items.question: What phrase describes adding resources to a failing effort to justify earlier spending?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The added resources are spent chasing an outcome the earlier money cannot buy back.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is throwing good money after bad. Each new commitment deepens the loss rather than recovering it.
items.lessonContent:
Recovery hopes can trap judgment.
Adding resources cannot undo past spending.
Stop and value the remaining options.
Treat each step on its own merits.
Share this: pause one effort where you are adding resources to recover a loss.

items.title: Decision at the Edge
items.question: What principle says decisions should compare only the additional costs and benefits of the next step?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Marginal analysis ignores what is already spent and asks what the next unit changes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is thinking at the margin. It is the natural antidote to letting sunk costs steer choices.
items.lessonContent:
Compare only what changes next.
Already-spent resources drop out.
Marginal reasoning isolates the real trade-off.
Ask what one more step buys.
Share this: evaluate one next step by its incremental costs and benefits alone.

items.title: Forgone Alternative
items.question: What concept captures the value of the best option you gave up by choosing one path?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Every choice forfeits alternatives, and their value belongs in the decision.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is opportunity cost. Ignoring it makes continued investment look cheaper than it is.
items.lessonContent:
Choosing one path forgoes others.
Count the best alternative's value.
Hidden costs shape real trade-offs.
Compare against your best next option.
Share this: name the best thing you give up by continuing one current effort.

items.title: Stopping the Bleed
items.question: What is the discipline of ending a failing effort before more resources are lost?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Recognising a dead end early preserves resources for better uses.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is cutting one's losses. It takes discipline because stopping feels like admitting defeat.
items.lessonContent:
Ending early can be the win.
Stopping limits further damage.
Pride makes exit feel like failure.
Reframe stopping as reallocation.
Share this: end one low-value commitment this week.

items.title: Would I Start Today
items.question: Which question best tests whether you are honouring a sunk cost?
choices: How much have I already spent
items.correctExplanation: Right. If you would not begin now, past spending is the only thing keeping you in.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is would I start this today. It strips away history and reveals the present value of continuing.
items.lessonContent:
Reset the decision to now.
Ask what you would choose fresh.
History should not be the decider.
Use the question at every fork.
Share this: apply the fresh-start question to one ongoing commitment.

items.title: Cost of Quitting
items.question: Why does ending a project feel more difficult than continuing it, even when continuing is worse?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Continuing keeps hope alive and defers the pain of acknowledging the loss.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is stopping makes the loss final. The emotional cost of closure, not the economics, often drives the choice.
items.lessonContent:
Closure has an emotional price.
Ongoing effort postpones the reckoning.
Separate feelings from arithmetic.
Name the real reason for continuing.
Share this: identify one effort kept alive mainly to avoid admitting a loss.

items.title: Justifying the Past
items.question: What psychological pressure pushes people to act in ways that justify earlier choices?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Admitting a bad decision is uncomfortable, so people bend later choices to defend it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is self-justification. Consistency with a past act can outweigh consistency with the present facts.
items.lessonContent:
We defend our prior choices.
Consistency can battle accuracy.
Notice when you argue to protect an image.
Allow yourself to have been wrong.
Share this: revise one position without defending the version you held before.

items.title: Public Promise
items.question: Why does announcing a commitment publicly make abandoning it harder?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Going back on a stated commitment invites embarrassment, which can outweigh a sensible exit.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is reputation raises the exit cost. The social stake keeps people in failing courses.
items.lessonContent:
Public stakes add pressure.
Reputation can lock in a bad course.
Separate your image from the decision.
Allow room to change your mind.
Share this: give yourself permission to reverse one announced plan if facts change.

items.title: Valuing What We Own
items.question: Why do people demand more to part with an object than they would pay to acquire it?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Once something is ours, losing it registers as a loss, which we weight more heavily.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the endowment effect. Ownership shifts the reference point and inflates the asking price.
items.lessonContent:
Ownership changes perceived value.
Losing feels larger than gaining.
Check whether attachment is inflating a price.
Value objectively where you can.
Share this: notice one possession you overvalue simply because it is yours.

items.title: Keeping Things As Is
items.question: What bias favours continuing with the current arrangement even when a better one is available?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Inaction preserves the present state and avoids the discomfort of change.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is status quo bias. Doing nothing feels neutral, though it is itself a choice with consequences.
items.lessonContent:
Inaction is not neutral.
Defaults quietly steer decisions.
Compare the current state to alternatives.
Choose actively, not by drift.
Share this: revisit one default you have never deliberately chosen.

items.title: Zero Based
items.question: What kind of review rebuilds a budget from scratch rather than from last year's figures?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Starting from nothing forces every expense to justify itself anew.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a zero-based review. It neutralises the pull of what was already committed.
items.lessonContent:
Rebuilding removes inherited assumptions.
Every item must earn its place.
History can entrench waste.
Periodically reset the baseline.
Share this: question one recurring expense as if it were new.

items.title: Group Pressure
items.question: Why can a team be more prone to escalation than an individual?
items.correctExplanation: Right. When no single person owns the failure, admitting it is easier to postpone.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is shared responsibility diffuses blame. Diffuse accountability makes cutting losses politically harder.
items.lessonContent:
Diffused blame weakens correction.
Shared decisions can share the blind spot.
Assign clear ownership of outcomes.
Make it safe to call a halt.
Share this: name who can unilaterally stop one effort you are part of.

items.title: Good After Bad
items.question: A person has spent years on a failing venture and continues only to justify the years spent. What is the error?
choices: Letting past effort drive present choice
items.correctAnswer: Letting past effort drive present choice
items.correctExplanation: Right. Effort already spent cannot be reclaimed, so it has no bearing on the next step.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is letting past effort drive present choice. The years are gone whether the venture continues or ends.
items.lessonContent:
Effort and money behave alike here.
Neither returns once spent.
Judge only from what is still ahead.
Separate commitment from evidence.
Share this: list one past effort you keep citing as a reason to continue.

items.title: Better Use
items.question: How should you judge resources already tied up in an uncertain project?
choices: By how long they have been used
By how much you like the project
items.correctExplanation: Right. What matters is what those resources could achieve elsewhere now.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is by their best alternative use. Original cost is history; current alternatives are the real comparison.
items.lessonContent:
Resources have present alternatives.
Compare next-best uses, not past prices.
Free up what serves better elsewhere.
Think forward, not backward.
Share this: name the best alternative use for one tied-up resource.

items.title: Just One More
items.question: A gambler keeps betting larger sums to recover earlier losses. Which pattern does this mirror?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Raising the stake to recover a loss adds risk instead of improving the odds.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is loss chasing. Each new bet is justified by the previous loss rather than by a genuine edge.
items.lessonContent:
Recovery attempts can deepen a hole.
Each new stake adds fresh risk.
Stop before the stakes dominate.
Separate past losses from future odds.
Share this: set a hard limit before one risky activity this week.

items.title: Cost Already Fixed
items.question: What term describes a cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Because it is unrecoverable, it is irrelevant to the next decision.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a sunk cost. Recognising it stops history from steering the present.
items.lessonContent:
Unrecoverable spending drops out of decisions.
Classification guides treatment.
Name the cost type before reasoning.
Keep marginal and sunk costs separate.
Share this: classify one cost in a decision you currently face.

items.title: Writing Off
items.question: What does it mean financially to write off a failed investment?
choices: Accept the loss and move on
items.correctAnswer: Accept the loss and move on
items.correctExplanation: Right. Recording the loss recognises reality and frees attention for better uses.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is accept the loss and move on. Pretending the loss is recoverable is what keeps resources trapped.
items.lessonContent:
Acknowledging a loss clears the ledger.
Denial keeps resources stuck.
Accept reality before reallocating.
Closure enables new action.
Share this: acknowledge one loss you have been avoiding naming.

items.title: Choosing Fresh
items.question: When should you review whether to continue an existing commitment?
choices: Whenever the option has real alternatives
Only after it has fully failed
items.correctAnswer: Whenever the option has real alternatives
items.correctExplanation: Right. If resources could go elsewhere, the continue-or-stop choice deserves regular review.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is whenever the option has real alternatives. Waiting for total failure wastes the remaining value.
items.lessonContent:
Review while options still exist.
Delay can squander the remaining value.
Schedule regular re-evaluation.
Do not wait for collapse.
Share this: schedule a review date for one current commitment.

items.title: Feelings as Guide
items.question: What is the risk of deciding to continue a project mainly because stopping would feel like a waste?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The aversion to feeling wasteful can outweigh a clear-eyed assessment of the returns.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is feelings override the evidence. The sense of waste is precisely the trap that keeps resources flowing to a failing effort.
items.lessonContent:
Emotion can masquerade as logic.
The dread of waste biases choices.
Check the numbers independently of the feeling.
Name the emotion before deciding.
Share this: notice one decision you are making to avoid feeling wasteful.

items.title: Cost and Worth
items.question: Why is the amount already spent a poor measure of whether to continue?
choices: It says nothing about future value
items.correctAnswer: It says nothing about future value
items.correctExplanation: Right. Continuation should depend on what remains to be gained, not on what has been spent.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it says nothing about future value. Past outlay and future return are independent questions.
items.lessonContent:
Past spending is not a forecast.
Future value stands alone.
Do not let cost history anchor the choice.
Evaluate the remaining opportunity.
Share this: judge one ongoing effort only by what it can still deliver.

items.title: Discomfort of Regret
items.question: Why do people sometimes continue bad decisions rather than face anticipated regret?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Deferring the pain of regret keeps a failing course going, even though the regret only grows.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is avoiding regret feels safer now. Short-term emotional relief can cost far more later.
items.lessonContent:
We dodge immediate discomfort.
Delayed regret often grows larger.
Weigh short-term relief against long-term cost.
Face the feeling to free the choice.
Share this: name one regret you are postponing to avoid discomfort.
